challenge.better_approach: Looked: bash's own parser is the precise judge, but proofgate has no bash AST and adding one is a dependency. Lifting heredoc bodies by delimiter is the smallest correct cut for the spellings measured.
challenge.hidden_assumption: That a heredoc fed to a non-shell runs no proof. `python3 - <<EOF` with runpy over a proof would; that is today unjudged in any spelling and is not made worse here.
challenge.prior_art: proofgate already judges `bash -c`/`sh -c`/`eval` strings as the command they are (72a37498c601); this applies the same rule to a heredoc fed to a shell.
challenge.real_collision: None: proofgate and its proof only; dda0's heredoc clause stays green, measured by its census.

answers.falsifier: `cat > f <<'EOF'` with a `python3 <proof>` body line passes unrewritten; `bash <<'EOS'` with the same body is rewritten; `bash <<-EOS` (tab-stripped) is rewritten; the existing 18 teeth stay green.
answers.how: Before cutting segments, proofgate lifts every heredoc body out of the command text. When the heredoc's command word is a shell (bash, sh, zsh, dash), the body is judged as the command it is, as `bash -c` already is; otherwise the body is data and is not judged. Teeth in bin/proofs/test_proof_gate.py.
answers.traces_to: Law 4 (the seal is physics, and a gate that fires on data teaches the hand to route around it) and Law 8; dda0e72b9c67's census, whose heredoc spelling must stay rewritten.
answers.what: proofgate judges a heredoc's body as commands only when the heredoc feeds a shell, so writing a script that names a proof to a file (cat > f <<EOF) passes unrewritten, while a heredoc fed to bash is still rewritten.
